title: Signs and symptoms words
blurb: Name the exact meaning of the fever, color, breathing, dizziness and wound words the HESI A2 pairs as traps.
question: “The patient was pale and diaphoretic and reported vertigo, but no syncope.” Can you tell sweating from urinating, spinning from fainting, and pale from blue fast enough to pick the right definition in under a minute?

teach.h: Words for what the body shows and feels
teach.body: Signs and symptoms words name the changes an ill person shows or feels: fever, sweating, skin color, breathing trouble, dizziness and wounds. Formally, they are the clinical terms used to record a patient's presenting problems. Plain English: these are the words a nurse writes in a chart to say how sick someone looks and feels. On the HESI A2 you see one of them in a short sentence and choose its meaning from four options that often belong to the same family.

items.label: Cyanosis (n)
items.sub: Bluish skin or lips: too little oxygen (cyan = blue)

items.label: Jaundice (n)
items.sub: Yellow skin and yellow whites of the eyes

items.label: Pallor (n)
items.sub: Unusual paleness: color drained from the skin

teach.caption: The HESI swaps these four constantly. Lock each word to one color.

head: Word (part of speech)
Meaning
Near miss
teach.caption: Example: “Diaphoretic and afebrile” means sweating heavily but without a fever.

teach.h: The dys- family: one prefix, four body jobs
teach.caption: Apnea (a- = without) is a pause in breathing. Dyspnea is breathing that continues, with effort.

teach.h: Scenario: Maya reads an urgent care note
teach.body: Maya, a nursing applicant shadowing at an urgent care center, reads this note: “Patient febrile and diaphoretic. Reports vertigo on standing; no syncope. Pallor noted. Three-centimeter laceration on left forearm with mild erythema and no purulent drainage.” She does not reach for a dictionary. She sorts each word into its family, then picks the exact meaning inside the family.

items: Febrile, diaphoretic: fever-and-sweat family. The patient has a fever and is sweating heavily.
Vertigo, no syncope: dizzy family. The room spins, but the patient has not fainted.
Pallor: color family. Pale, not blue (cyanosis), yellow (jaundice) or red (erythema).
Laceration, erythema, not purulent: wound family. A torn cut, red at the edges, with no pus.

teach.text: The HESI builds wrong options from the same family. Vertigo (spinning) and syncope (fainting) both follow a dizzy spell; cyanosis and pallor both describe a sick-looking face; dyspnea and dysphagia share a prefix. Knowing the family only narrows it to two. Learn the one detail that separates the pair.

items: Colors: cyanosis blue, jaundice yellow, pallor pale, erythema red.
Febrile = fever, afebrile = no fever, pyrexia = fever, diaphoresis = heavy sweating, emesis = vomiting.
dys- = difficult: dyspnea breathing, dysphagia swallowing, dysphasia speech, dysuria urination.
Vertigo spins, syncope faints; lethargic is drowsy, malaise is a vague unwell feeling.
Laceration torn, abrasion scraped, contusion bruised; purulent = pus, pruritus = itching.

summary: You can now give the exact meaning of the common fever, color, breathing, dizziness, skin and wound words. You can also separate the look-alike pairs the HESI A2 uses as distractors, such as vertigo and syncope or pruritus and purulent.

A.q: Mrs. Patel noticed a fine tremor in her hands when she tried to thread a needle. What is the best definition of the word “tremor” in this sentence?
A.why: A tremor is involuntary shaking or trembling, which makes fine work such as threading a needle hard.

whyNot.0: Numbness and tingling describe altered sensation, not shaking.
whyNot.2: A cramp is a painful, sustained muscle tightening, not trembling.
whyNot.3: A swollen growth is a tumor, the sound-alike of tremor.

A.q: The newborn's jaundice was easiest to see in the whites of his eyes on the third day. What is the best definition of the word “jaundice” in this sentence?
A.why: Jaundice is a yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes.

whyNot.1: Redness of the skin is erythema.

A.q: Mr. Reyes was pale and showed diaphoresis, so the nurse wiped his forehead and checked his blood sugar. What is the best definition of the word “diaphoresis” in this sentence?
A.why: Diaphoresis is heavy sweating, which is why the nurse wiped his forehead.

whyNot.1: Increased urination is diuresis, a look-alike word.
whyNot.3: A sense of unease is dysphoria, a sound-alike.

B.q: After walking to the mailbox, Mr. Ford had dyspnea and sat on the porch step for several minutes. What is the best definition of the word “dyspnea” in this sentence?
B.why: Dyspnea is difficult or labored breathing: dys- (difficult) + -pnea (breathing).

B.q: Ms. Allen has had two episodes of syncope this month, both while standing in a hot kitchen. What is the best definition of the word “syncope” in this sentence?
B.why: Syncope is fainting: a brief loss of consciousness, often from heat or standing too long.

whyNot.1: A spinning sensation is vertigo, the classic partner trap.
whyNot.2: Nausea is a sick stomach; she may feel it, but syncope is fainting.
whyNot.3: A muscle spasm is an involuntary contraction, not a loss of consciousness.

B.q: Kayla's contusion turned purple the day after the soccer ball struck her thigh. What is the best definition of the word “contusion” in this sentence?
B.why: A contusion is a bruise: bleeding under unbroken skin, which turns purple.

whyNot.0: A jagged cut is a laceration.
whyNot.3: A strain is an overstretched muscle; it does not turn the skin purple.

C.q: Which word means a feeling that the heart is pounding, racing or skipping beats?
C.why: A palpitation is a feeling that the heart is beating fast, hard or irregularly.

whyNot.0: Palpation is examination by touch, the look-alike that differs by two letters.
whyNot.1: Perfusion is blood flow through tissue, not a feeling.

C.q: Apart from a low-grade fever, Mr. Kent described only malaise and a poor appetite. What is the best definition of the word “malaise” in this sentence?
C.why: Malaise is a vague, general feeling of being unwell or uncomfortable.

whyNot.0: A specific illness is a malady, a look-alike word.
whyNot.1: An urge to vomit is nausea, a more specific symptom.
whyNot.2: Ill will is malice, a sound-alike.

C.q: The nurse applied firm pressure to stop the hemorrhage from the patient's scalp wound. What is the best definition of the word “hemorrhage” in this sentence?
C.why: A hemorrhage is heavy or uncontrolled bleeding, which pressure is meant to stop.

whyNot.1: Blood pooled under the skin is a hematoma.
whyNot.2: A swollen vein near the anus is a hemorrhoid, a look-alike.
whyNot.3: A deep infection may be an abscess; pressure here stops bleeding.

reteach.title: Paint chips and memory hooks
reteach.question: Picture a hardware store's paint chips: “Cyan Sky,” “Jaundice Gold,” “Pale Pallor,” “Erythema Red.” If every symptom word had a hook like that, would you mix them up?

blocks.h: Hang each word on something you already know
blocks.body: You never confuse sky blue with lemon yellow because each name points to a picture. Do the same with symptom words. Cyanosis: cyan ink in a printer. Erythema: erythrocyte, the red blood cell. Syncope: you “sink” to the floor. Vertigo: the world turns like a merry-go-round. Pruritus: “prickly” itch. Purulent: “pus” sits in the first syllable.

blocks.text: A hook is a memory aid, not the definition. On test day, choose the option that matches the meaning column, not the hook.

explain.body: Four nouns name skin color changes: cyanosis (bluish, from too little oxygen), jaundice (yellow skin and eyes), pallor (unusual paleness) and erythema (redness). Flush is a temporary reddening of the face, almost the opposite of pallor.

test.q: Under the bright clinic lights, the nurse noticed Deshawn's pallor and asked when he had last eaten. What is the best definition of the word “pallor” in this sentence?
test.why: Pallor is unusual paleness of the skin.

whyNot.2: A flushed face is red, nearly the opposite of pallor.

explain.body: Febrile means having a fever; afebrile means without one. Pyrexia is the noun for fever. Diaphoresis is heavy sweating (not diuresis, more urine). Nausea is the urge to vomit; emesis is the vomiting itself.

test.q: Because the infant was febrile, the clinic moved her appointment to the front of the schedule. What is the best definition of the word “febrile” in this sentence?

whyNot.0: Without a fever is afebrile, the opposite.
whyNot.1: Dehydration is a loss of body water, a different problem.
whyNot.3: Weak and frail is feeble, a sound-alike.

explain.body: Dyspnea is difficult breathing and apnea is a pause in breathing. Vertigo is a spinning sensation; syncope is fainting. Lethargic means drowsy and sluggish; malaise is a vague unwell feeling.

test.q: Mr. Sato's vertigo began when he tilted his head back to look at the ceiling fan. What is the best definition of the word “vertigo” in this sentence?
test.why: Vertigo is the sensation that oneself or the surroundings are spinning.

whyNot.1: A headache is pain, not a sense of motion.
whyNot.2: Blurred vision is a change in sight, not spinning.

explain.body: A laceration is a torn, jagged cut; an abrasion is a scrape; a contusion is a bruise; a lesion is any abnormal area of tissue. Purulent means containing pus; pruritus is itching.

test.q: The surgical site was red and purulent, so the doctor ordered a wound culture. What is the best definition of the word “purulent” in this sentence?
test.why: Purulent means containing or discharging pus.

whyNot.2: Free bleeding would be a hemorrhage; purulent refers to pus.
